# NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops: What They Are and Who They're For

> **In short:** NVIDIA's RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are now available to buy. NVIDIA says they're built to run AI models and AI agents on your own machine, alongside image, video and 3D tools, and they can keep working while your laptop is away.

If you've heard people talk about running AI "locally" and wondered whether it's for you, this announcement is a useful place to start. Running AI on your own computer, instead of only on a remote server, changes what you can do and how your files travel.

## What the desktops are

These are small Windows desktop computers, sometimes called mini PCs. NVIDIA says they combine a processor (the CPU, the general-purpose brain of a computer) with a graphics processor (the GPU, which is especially good at the heavy math AI models need).

The main specs NVIDIA lists include:

- A 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU
- An NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores (the small processing units inside the GPU that do many calculations at once)
- Up to 128GB of unified memory, which is memory that the processor and graphics chip share
- Ten-gigabit Ethernet, a fast wired network connection for moving large files

NVIDIA says the system can deliver up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. A petaflop is one quadrillion calculations per second, and it is NVIDIA's own figure, so treat it as the company's claim.

## Why running AI locally matters

Most AI tools you use today, such as a chatbot in your browser, send your request to a company's cloud servers. A local model runs on your own hardware instead.

NVIDIA says this has two practical benefits:

- **Your files stay on your PC.** Code and files processed locally don't have to be sent to the cloud.
- **You avoid per-token charges.** Cloud AI services often bill for each token (a small chunk of text, roughly a word or part of a word) that the AI reads and writes. Running supported models locally skips those charges for those tasks.

NVIDIA also describes a feature called Switchyard, which sends simple tasks to the local model and complex reasoning to the cloud. The idea is to keep everyday work on the desktop and save cloud use for harder problems.

## A dedicated machine for always-on tasks

NVIDIA says these desktops are designed to run AI agents, which are programs that can carry out tasks on your behalf, such as sorting files or running scheduled jobs. Because the desktop is separate from your laptop, it can keep those tasks going while you travel or use your laptop for something else.

Software support is growing too. NVIDIA mentions native Windows versions of several Adobe apps, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and InDesign. It also says Blender 5.3 adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction, an NVIDIA feature that cleans up lighting in 3D previews.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you edit family photos or video, or like to experiment with AI image tools, a dedicated machine keeps heavy work off your everyday laptop.
- **For your business or work**: If you're a freelancer, designer, video editor or developer, NVIDIA's list of supported Adobe and creative tools may matter most. Check that your specific software and models are supported before you buy.
- **If you're just getting started**: You don't need this hardware to learn AI. Start with a cloud AI tool, and consider local hardware only once you know which tasks you repeat often.
- **If you already use it**: If you already run local models, NVIDIA's announcement points to the Hermes Agent and NemoClaw blueprints for building agents, and Unsloth for fine-tuning (training an existing model on your own examples).

For current prices and configurations, check the official pricing pages from ASUS, Dell or MSI. NVIDIA says Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, are coming soon.

## Wrap-up

RTX Spark compact desktops are small Windows computers that NVIDIA designed for local AI, creative work and always-on tasks. If you do lots of image, video or development work, they're worth understanding. Your next step: list the AI or creative tasks you repeat each week, then check whether the software you use is on NVIDIA's supported list.
